pages.text:
At 6:47, the dinosaur climbed on my chest.

"RAAAAWR," he said.

I did not move. I kept my eyes shut and lay there with my arms stiff at my sides, breathing slow and pretending I was a statue made of heavy, tired stone. Gus roared again, closer this time. He nudged my nose with his snout, which smelled like green plastic and old laundry.

"Max. Wake up. It is Saturday."

"I'm listening," I whispered.

He climbed off and stood on the floor, looking up at me with one eye, confused, like a dog who has dropped a stick and lost interest. He left.

I got up and pulled my hood over my head, the strings dangling like dead vines. I walked to the garage, where the air was cool against my face. Waffles was waiting by the door. He did not bark or steal. Instead, he trotted to my feet, lay down, and rested his chin on his paws. He watched me with a look that said, *I am here. You can be sad. I will not fix it.*

It was the first comfort I had ever received that did not come with a string attached.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie walks through a garage doorway while Waffles, a chubby corgi, lies on the floor with his chin on his paws, watching him calmly; soft morning light, cardboard boxes in the background.

pages.text:
At 1:15, the green Buick pulled into the driveway, and the horn played a tune that sounded like a tuba having a severe hiccup.

Grandma Bea stepped out. She was tiny, wearing big round sunglasses and red lipstick that looked painted on with a marker. In her hands, she carried a laundry basket. Inside the basket sat the cuckoo clock.

I followed her into the house. She walked fast, her gold bangles jingling against her wrist like a bag of loose change. She headed for the front hall, where the last empty hook waited.

I stopped her.

"Nonna," I said.

She turned around. I looked at her. I did not ask if she was tired. I did not ask about the drive. I asked the only question that mattered.

"What was your worst day?"

She stopped walking. She took off her sunglasses. For the first time in the whole book, I saw her eyes. They were brown, and they were old, and they were kind.

"I am listening, caro," she said.

"I have been having a truly awful time," I said. "And I don't know how to make it stop."
pages.image: Max stands in a hallway facing Grandma Bea, a tiny woman in big sunglasses and red lipstick, who holds a laundry basket containing a wooden clock; Max has his hood up, looking tired.

pages.text:
She set the basket down. She did not hang the clock. She sat on it, the way you sit on a suitcase when you are tired of carrying it.

"When I was eleven," she said, "I was moving from Naples to Ohio. I was furious. At the plane. At the cold. At my mother. I was standing in an airport. It was bare. There were no plants. There was no sun. Just concrete and bad coffee."

She picked up her hands and counted on her fingers.

"Then a man in a raincoat walked up to me. He had a peach. He cut it in half. He handed me one. It was the best peach I ever tasted. Juicy. Sweet. It tasted like summer."

She leaned forward.

"I sat on my suitcase. I ate the peach. And I thought, this day is going to be terrible either way. I got to choose whether I was terrible in it."
pages.image: Grandma Bea sits on a laundry basket in a hallway, holding a small wooden clock, looking at Max with a gentle, serious expression; the hallway is empty with bare walls.

pages.text:
"That's it?" I said. "That's the wisdom? A peach?"

She laughed, a loud, barking sound that seemed to shake the whole front hall, and her gold bangles jingled wildly against her wrist. "It is not the peach, caro. It is that I decided before the peach came. You think I was happy when I got the peach? No. I was happy because I ate the peach on purpose."

She stood up, brushing imaginary lint from her skirt, and reached out to pat my cheek. Her hand was warm, dry, and smelled faintly of perfume and old paper. "Happiness isn't what you get at the end of a day. It is what you bring to the front of it."

Then she hung the clock on the last hook in the hall. It ticked. It did not speak. It just ticked, steady and indifferent, like a metronome counting off a beat that no one was dancing to. I looked at the bird, and the bird looked at me with its painted, angry eyebrows. It did not care about my problems or my moving truck or my 1,700 miles of cactus. That total lack of concern was, I decided, the best part of the whole thing.
pages.image: Grandma Bea hangs a wooden cuckoo clock on a hook in a hallway, patting Max's cheek gently; Max looks up at the clock, which has a small painted bird with a crooked beak.

pages.text:
I sat on the floor under the clock and stared at Gerald.

I had lived seventy-two Saturdays. I had been asking the wrong question of the clock. I had been asking, *How do I make this stop?* But the question was never about stopping. The question was about being.

How do I want to be in it?

I realized I had been waiting for the day to be perfect so I could be happy. But the day was never going to be perfect. It was always going to be messy, and loud, and ending.

I could choose to be angry in it. Or I could choose to be glad.

I looked at my hands. They were still.

That night, at 11:59, I did not make a wish. I went to bed. And at 6:47...
pages.image: Max sits on the floor in a hallway, looking up at a wooden cuckoo clock on the wall; the small painted bird is visible in the clock's door; soft, quiet lighting.
